data.name: Dino Scourge
data.detailed_description:
This game has been disabled for the time being. This game will be revamped and changed in the coming months...

Why we fight

Aeons ago, dinosaurs were expelled from Earth due to their eating habits.

Dinosaurs were never extinct like humans thought though, they are still out there.

They discovered Earth has Rabbits, and love eating them.

Humans have genetically engineered Rabbits into excreting starship fuel.

Genetic engineering secrets were permanently lost due to wikipedia fire of 2666.

Humans must protect the remaining genetically engineered Rabbits, or all hope is lost.

Gameplay

Experience this top down online arcade style shooter, where you will be blasting through endless waves of Space Dinosaurs whilst protecting a starship full of rabbits on their long journey to safety through space.

Select a pilot from 4 different classes and improve your pilot's skills with experience points gained from fighting each level.

Select up to 4 special abilities to be used in each level.

Equip your ship with equipment collected from the levels, and modify each weapon with attachments which can alter your weapon in unique and crazy ways. From making weapons pierce all enemies to turning them into automatic turrets.

Features

Highly customisable ship system

Crafting Station to improve items

High score table

Skill tree

Seeing Dinosaurs swim through space

reviews.review:
Dino Scourge is a quirky top-down space shooter that combines arcade combat, role-playing progression, and an entertainingly absurd science-fiction premise. Developed and published by Scourgey Works, the game revolves around fighting waves of extraterrestrial dinosaurs while protecting a spacecraft carrying humanity's most valuable resource: genetically engineered rabbits. Although its concept sounds ridiculous, that unusual combination gives the experience a distinctive personality. Beneath the humor lies an ambitious collection of customization mechanics, character upgrades, and defensive combat objectives. Unfortunately, its unfinished development and uncertain accessibility significantly diminish what could otherwise have been an enjoyable independent action game.

The story immediately establishes its comedic identity through an alternative explanation for dinosaur extinction. Rather than disappearing from existence, dinosaurs were supposedly banished from Earth because of their excessive eating habits. After surviving in outer space, they discover that rabbits inhabit their former home planet and develop an appetite for them. The situation becomes particularly dangerous because humanity has genetically modified rabbits to produce spacecraft fuel. With the scientific knowledge behind this achievement permanently lost, protecting these animals becomes essential for civilization's survival. This wonderfully nonsensical premise provides an amusing backdrop for the action without requiring an elaborate narrative.

Gameplay focuses on piloting a spacecraft through continuous waves of hostile dinosaurs while defending a vulnerable transport vessel. Unlike traditional shooters that emphasize eliminating enemies for points, the escort objective introduces an additional layer of responsibility. Players must theoretically balance offensive aggression with defensive positioning, preventing enemies from overwhelming their precious cargo. The top-down perspective suits this style of combat by offering a broad view of approaching threats. However, the available information does not establish how varied the enemy encounters are or whether the defensive mechanics maintain their appeal throughout extended sessions.

Character progression is one of the game's more promising elements. Players can choose between four pilot classes, each contributing to the intended role-playing structure. Defeating enemies rewards experience points that can improve pilot abilities, while a skill tree provides opportunities for further specialization. Players may also select up to four special abilities for individual levels, introducing strategic decisions before combat begins. These mechanics potentially encourage experimentation with different builds and combat approaches. Nevertheless, without detailed information about class balance and ability interactions, it remains difficult to determine how much meaningful variety the progression system actually delivers.

Ship customization adds another interesting dimension. Equipment collected during missions can be installed to improve combat effectiveness, while weapon attachments modify how individual armaments function. Some upgrades allow projectiles to penetrate enemies, whereas others transform weapons into automated turrets. These modifications suggest that players can create substantially different offensive configurations rather than simply increasing damage statistics. A crafting station further supports equipment improvement, giving loot collection a practical purpose. Combined with the high-score system, these features establish a potentially satisfying cycle of fighting, collecting, upgrading, and attempting increasingly successful runs.

The presentation embraces an unconventional mixture of futuristic technology and prehistoric creatures. Dinosaurs swimming through space create an inherently humorous visual concept, and the arcade perspective allows the action to remain the primary focus. However, visual creativity alone cannot compensate for incomplete technical refinement. The developers acknowledged that optimization, bug fixing, and general polishing required additional work. Voice acting was also identified as an unfinished component, while multiplayer and matchmaking were planned rather than implemented. Consequently, the game's intended scope is considerably more ambitious than its documented single-player Early Access functionality.

Its development condition represents the biggest obstacle to a stronger recommendation. Steam warns that the developers have not provided updates for more than seven years, while the game's description explicitly states that it has been disabled pending substantial changes. This creates serious uncertainty about whether the experience remains accessible. The requirement for a separate login to the game's server further complicates matters, particularly because successful authentication depends on infrastructure outside Steam. Although the game is free to play, eliminating any purchase cost, that advantage becomes less meaningful if players cannot reliably access its gameplay.

Steam Deck compatibility is currently Unknown or Unverified, with no confirmed Verified or Playable classification established in the available listing. The published system requirements target Windows, and the game requires DirectX 11 alongside a broadband internet connection. Its relatively modest hardware requirements suggest that raw processing power might not be the main concern, but compatibility with Proton, handheld controls, and the external login system remains unconfirmed. Steam Deck owners should therefore avoid assuming that the game will function properly without additional testing.

Dino Scourge ultimately feels like an imaginative project whose ideas are more compelling than its documented state of completion. The combination of absurd storytelling, dinosaur-themed space combat, customizable ships, pilot classes, skill progression, and equipment crafting provides a surprisingly interesting foundation. Its greatest strength is the potential interaction between these systems, allowing players to develop personalized combat strategies within a humorous arcade setting. However, missing features, unresolved technical concerns, prolonged development inactivity, and uncertain server functionality prevent it from becoming an easy recommendation. Players fascinated by unusual independent games may appreciate its creativity, but anyone seeking a polished and dependable shooter should approach it cautiously.

Its originality and promising progression mechanics earn credit, but the unfinished execution and uncertain playability substantially weaken its overall appeal. This score reflects an assessment of its documented features and condition rather than a verified hands-on playthrough.

Rating: 5/10
